rv.q: This is a big, bold, entertaining swing at major issues, led with considerable star power.
Yet it is excitingly staged theatre with an ambition as bold as Yvonne's, seeking to say so much about women, race and the media that still feels incredibly timely.
Still, it's a big, brash thriller with some solid performances - particularly Toussaint's Pat, though big-name Wright is good as the driven but awkward Yvonne.

Clint Dyer's flashy, pacy revival of this intelligent whodunnit resurrects a different era – one in which newspapers still owned the narrative, and blogs hinted at a more democratic future. It’s a fascinating watch, offering few easy takeaways.
But, amid the zig-zagging story telling, the drama itself goes missing.
Sadly, it doesn't add much to the conversation.
Dyer’s direction is superbly confident, and beautifully realised as characters speak and argue in parallel scenes.
All the same there's a lot here to like and even linger over.
However, all these promising strands fail to cohere, adding little new to the conversation and leading to a rushed, open-ended conclusion.

Both the play The Story and reporter Yvonne’s big story suffer from the same issue: a great idea smothered by an overworked device that increasingly becomes a distraction instead of the instrument of the author.

While there are some intriguing and insightful remarks about the injustices faced by black people in American journalism as well as in wider society, the play takes too long to make the point, already known to the savvy and discerning, that mainstream media is not to be trusted.
This is a promising premise, but the play, despite updates to the script for this revival, falls strangely flat.
As a thriller, it never takes off, and the melodrama of the second half isn't really very convincing.

It is not a perfect play, the ending not entirely satisfying; often the quest for authenticity blurs the narrative, (in the interval several were muttering in puzzlement). But Toussaint is remarkable in her grand intensity, and Wright manages to just about convince us of what Yvonne is hiding.
There is a lot of potential to be found in The Story, and it is far from a bad show.
The Story is intense and brilliant with amazing acting, a clever and pacey script and a mystery that keeps you questioning what you think you know.
Although I was left questioning the play's conclusion, it's a compelling story, with great performances and a visually exciting production.

cn.t: Wilson's newsroom thriller about race and journalistic ethics delivers kinetic energy and strong performances from Wright and Toussaint, but critics find the play uneven, with a disjointed second half that turns preachy despite its timely themes.
